nodes.title: Summary/Abstract
nodes.body: [caption]The Spotted Seatrout, Cynoscion nebulosus.  Illustration by Diana Rome Peebles 1998 [/caption]

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Scientific Name: Cynoscion nebulosus
Common Name: spotted Seatrout

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
Class: Actinopterygii
Order: Perciformes
Family: Sciaenidae

Note: The American Fisheries Society has listed the common name spotted seatrout since 1960 (1911 1912 1913 1914).
A reference for Scientific Name = (Cuvier 1830)
A reference for Family = (1702)
Superclass: Osteichthyes
Subclass: Neopterygii
Infraclass: Teleostei
Superorder: Acanthopterygii

nodes.title: Synonyms
nodes.body:
Jordan and Evermann 1896 compiled the following synonymy (1834):
Labrus squeteague var. maculatus, Mitchill, Trans. Lit. and Phil. Soc. 1815,396, New York; not Labrus maculatus, Bloch.
Otolithus nebulosus, Cuvier and Valenciennes, Hist. Nat. Poiss., v, 79, 1830, locality unknown.
Otolithus carolinensis, Cuvier and Carolinensis, Hist. Nat. Poiss., ix, 475, 1833, South Carolina; Giinther, Cat., 11, 306, 1860.
Otolithus drummondi, Richardson, Fauna Bor. -Am., Fish., 70, 1836, New Orleans; Girard, U.S. and Mex. Bound. Survey, Zool., 12, pl. 6, 1859; Gunther, Cat., l t 307, 1860.
Cestreus carolinensis, Gronow, Cat. Fish., Ed. Gray, 49, 1854.
Cynoscion carolinensis, Jordan and Gilbert, Proc. U.S. Nat. Mus. 1878,377.
Cynoscion maculatus, Jordan and Gilbert, Proc. U.S. Nat. Mus. 1882,285; Jordan and Gilbert, Synopsis, 581, 1883; Jordan and Swain, Proc. U.S. Nat. Mus. 1884,233.
Cestreus nebulosus, Jordan and Eigenmann, l.c., 368, 1889.

Other Common Names: speckled trout (315 664 835); spotted sea trout (1 834); spotted trout (315 543); squeteague (543); spotted squeteague (315 19 10 19 1 8); spotted weakfish (315 791 1834 191 6 19 18); simon trout (315 834); speck (664); southern squeteague (834); speckles (3 15 19 18); salmon trout (315). Seatrout; black trout.
Spanish: corvina pinta (1635); trucha de mar (1703 1916); corvina (1916); curvina (19 16); corvinata pintada (791); corbina (1925).
Maya: Utz cai (1925).
French: acoupa pintade (79 119 16 19 18).
Portuguese: corvinata pintada (19 17 19 1 8).

Taxonomic characteristics:
Adults: Dark grey above with bluish reflections and numerous black spots on back, upper sides, and soft part of dorsal and anal fins; spinous portion of dorsal fin dusky, other fins yellowish or pale; maxilla not extending beyond hind margin of eye; soft portion of dorsal fin up to basal third of fin and caudal fin covered with small scales (791 1704). Spots on back and upper sides are larger in spotted seatrout than in the weakfish, Cynoscion regalis, in which also the small spots form faint irregular, oblique streaks along the scale rows. Protein taxonomy was described by Weinstein (1975), and Weinstein and Yerger (1976).
Similar Species: The weakfish, Cynoscion regalis (Bloch & Schneider, 1801).
Evolutionary Relationships:  Unpublished preliminary mtDNA studies (Dr. John R. Gold, Texas A&M University, cited in 1678) found extremely low genetic variation among several areas of the Gulf. The low variability shows an inconsistent geographic pattern in the occurrence of mtDNA haplotypes. Inferences from an island isolate model suggested that since genetic variability is quite low (1773 1665), an exchange of only 5% of the breeding population would be needed among estuaries to maintain the observed genetic uniformity of spotted seatrout (1773).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall: Coastal waters from Massachusetts to Isla del Carmen in the lower Bay of Campeche, Mexico, including the Gulf of Mexico (402 461 788 791 792 1835 1847 191 9 1920 1921 1922 1923) and Holbox Island, Quintana Roo, Mexico (1635 1636). It is rare north of Delaware, and the center of abundance is from Florida to Texas, including Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and south Texas
(327 402 543 762 1738).

nodes.title: By State
nodes.body:
Within Florida: Distributed throughout Florida's coastal and estuarine waters (792 891 1281 1284).
By Stock: Conflicting conclusions have been reached regarding the presence of stock subdivisions in Florida and the Gulf of Mexico (1677). Tagging and growth studies in Florida postulated that separate subpopulations occur in Florida (1752 1753). These findings were also supported by blood serum and eye lens protein electrophoretic patterns. These showed eight independent stocks; seven along the Gulf coast and one in Indian River, Florida (1290).  Correspondingly, shape analysis of scales and otoliths suggested that separate stocks occurred in Texas bays (1749). However, protein electrophoresis patterns found in Texas (1665 1773) and growth estimates from Apalachicola Bay, Charlotte Harbor, and Indian River Lagoon, Florida (1678) do not support the previously postulated subpopulations found in Florida. The Florida Marine Fisheries Commission has divided Florida into three regions and the fish within each of those regions are considered operational stocks. The boundaries of the east coast region are the Florida-Georgia border and the Dade-Monroe county line, the boundaries of the southwest region are the Dade-Monroe county line and the Pinellas-Pasco county line, and the boundaries of the northwest region are the Pinellas-Pasco county line and the Florida-Alabama border (1678).  A preliminary evaluation of the use of calcified structures by Colura and King (1989) to separate stocks was promising. The results indicated that shape and growth characteristics of scale and otolith were useful to separate Texas stocks (1740).
By Estuary: Tampa Bay distribution has been analyzed based on extensive spring and fall sampling conducted by the Fisheries Independent Monitoring Program, FDEP’s FMRI. An index of relative abundance classified one-minute grids of latitude and longitude into zero-catch CPUE, low-to-medium CPUE, and high CPUE. Maps were prepared for length class, gear, and season (1647).

nodes.title: Spatial Strategy
nodes.body:
Spotted seatrout complete their entire life cycle in inshore waters (751). Year-round resident of estuaries but adults occasionally move offshore along the beaches to avoid extreme cold (157 293 430 543 701 751 1284 1285). In Georgia, spotted seatrout are found throughout the estuaries, from the upper tidal marshes to the beaches and outer bars. They seem to prefer the shallow waters along the banks of tidal creeks, rivers, and sounds near oyster beds, and along the beaches near inlets (430). Hildebrand and Cable (1825) reported that spotted seatrout in North Carolina are taken throughout the year in the shallow waters of the estuaries and sounds. In Texas spotted seatrout prefers clear bays and lagoons, and stretches of beach near passes (543). Eggs are found from marine to estuarine environments and are buoyant or demersal depending on salinity; generally in association with grass beds at or near passes. They are also found in areas with fine to medium texture detritus devoid of vegetation (614). Larvae are demersal in deep channels with shell rubble or in bottom vegetation (701).

The eggs are pelagic (>30 ppt) or demersal (25 ppt) depending on salinity (468 1637 1638), larvae are pelagic and after 4-7 days become demersal (708). Juveniles and adults are demersal. Spotted seatrout posses definite diel pattern of metabolic activity, with increased activity occurring at night (741).

Spotted seatrout in Florida tend to spawn and live in a particular estuary, and to move only short distances. It is considered non migratory (701). A tagging study on Florida's west coast recovered over 95% of the fish tagged within 30 miles from their point of release (1288 1734). Large individuals often seek cooler deeper water during the summer; in the winter they seek deeper, warmer waters or move out to the nearshore Gulf of Mexico (543 255 701). Tagging studies have shown that few fish leave their natal estuary and that spotted seatrout seldom moved more than 50 km (30 mi) from the tagging site (1042 1287 1288 1289 1734). Little is known about the distribution of larvae less than 10 mm TL.  Jannke (354) and King (1837) reported finding larvae 5-6 mm TL being transported on flood tides through passes connecting the Gulf of Mexico and inside waters. Numerous authors have cited an apparent preference of postlarval and juvenile spotted seatrout for shallow, vegetated estuarine areas (543 468 549). Tabb reported schooling at a size of 25-50 mm or 6-8 weeks old (701). Juveniles 75-100 mm form schools of 5 to 50 members (549) and continue this schooling behavior to age V or VI (701). By age VI, apparently most males have died and the remaining females adopt a semi-solitary existence (701). Juveniles remain in the estuary nursery areas at least through the warmer months. Pearson (543) suggested that the young seldom move into the Gulf until mature, but that "many adults linger around the entrances to the passes at all times of the year."
Mobility: Spotted seatrout are not considered migratory in Florida (701); they usually do not move more than 48 km (30 mi) from tagging sites, and they rarely leave their natal estuary (1288 1831 1752 1895 1707 1289 1697). However, some long-distance movements have been reported.  These movements appeared to be associated with changes in temperature and salinity (1288).  Also, in the Galveston Bay System, Texas during late spring and summer spotted seatrout moved towards the Gulf of Mexico then returned to the tagging site in the fall. This movement perhaps is related to feeding or is part of a spawning migration (1642 1644). Fall emigration of spotted seatrout to the deeper, warmer waters of the bays or Gulf is apparent, but less pronounced than in other Gulf fishes (701 1288). Pearson (543) reported that large fish in the Gulf of Mexico enter bays in early spring to feed. There is limited movement within Everglades National Park (1278 1435 1437 1775 1777). It has been suggested for Texas and Florida that a nearshore, westerly directed transport system moving eggs and larvae along the series of closely spaced bay systems may facilitate gene exchange between bay populations (1665).

Seasonal movement and migration of spotted seatrout were studied in Georgia's St. Andrew estuarine systems. 2,000 creel-sized fish were tagged and released during 1979-1981. About 15% of the fish were recovered. Preliminary indications are that spotted seatrout in Georgia remain within a particular estuarine system during their adult life. Spotted seatrout apparently move in and out of the open sounds seasonally enroute to creeks and rivers in fall and winter, and out to beaches in spring and early summer. Most movements were short range, averaging 8.9 km, although one fish traveled 105 km. The greatest time at large was 747 days (1767). Tagging studies in Mississippi indicated that spotted seatrout did not move farther than 25 km from the location of release (1769).

Symbiotic: Not symbiotic.
Schooling: Large juveniles and adults form small schools (543).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Substrate (by life stage):
The juveniles are found largely over bottom types with medium to soft, mud-detritus substrates (559). The preferred habitat in Louisiana is along relatively shallow marsh edges of small, saline water bodies in Spartina alterniflora dominated areas (559). Juveniles and adults are demersal completing entire life cycle in inshore waters (751 741). Adults also occur in surf zones of barrier islands particularly in the fall (553). Spotted seatrout in south Florida prefers brackish shallow water habitats with extensive  submerged vegetation, such as Thalassia testudinum and Halodule wrightii adjacent to deep waters (3-6 m), that can be used as refuges from the cold and during low tides in the winter (1284 581 1778). In contrast, although such habitat in the northern Gulf is scarce, spotted seatrout are still common there (163).

Submerged Vegetation (by life stage):
The substrate for larvae is highly variable; they are generally associated with grassbeds but are also found in unvegetated backwaters (47 524 543 700 741 1276 1284 1647).  Also collected along the beaches in the surf zone (157 430), and in small tidal pools, intertidal creeks, bayous, and moderately deep channels (157 430 700 701 1276 1286). In Tampa Bay, larvae were collected over grass beds in the middle and lower bay and in quiet slow-moving freshwater-influenced rivers, bayous and tidal creeks with sand or mud bottoms (1276 1647).

The Juveniles and adults are primarily associated with seagrasses (1276 1278 993) but also are common over shallow muddy areas, oil platforms and shell reefs (47 157 327 430 543 848 1281 1284). Both Rutherford et al. (1278) and Chester and Thayer (1433) found juvenile seatrout associated with increased S. jiliforme biomass. In the Indian River lagoon, Traxler & Gilmore (In prep.) determined that juvenile seatrout (< 75 mm, SL) prefer H. wrightii.

Darnell (163) points out that most investigators link spotted seatrout to seagrass beds.  McMichael and Peters (1131) suggest that seagrass is the primary habitat for juveniles, with 78% of all juveniles having been collected over seagrass areas. Miles (468) suggested that young spotted seatrout seek protection among submerged and emergent vegetation in shallow waters.

Depth Distribution (by life stage): Need information.

nodes.title: WATER COLUMN HABITAT
nodes.body:
Temperature (by lifestage):
The Larvae Taniguchi found a temperature range of 23 - 33 C for larvae in South Florida (708 1780). Young-of-year Spotted seatrout 18-130 mm SL were collected by Jannke (354) in water with temperature range 12 – 29 C at Cedar Key, Florida; in the Everglades National Park from 16-32 C by Reid (581) and Jannke (354). The optimum temperature for adult fish was reported from 15 to 27 C (1778). The temperature range is slightly higher than the 20 – 30 C    range reported in Texas (20). The large-scale spawning of spotted seatrout begins in the Everglades National Park when water temperature is near 24 C (354 1242). In east-central Florida, spotted seatrout spawn when temperature was near 27 C (1778). Spawning rapidly declined when temperatures were raised above 30 C (354 1778). Fall spawning peaks in the Everglades National Park failed to materialize when early fall temperatures remained above 30 C (354).

Eggs and yolk-sac larvae have an optimal temperature of 28 C, but have been hatched experimentally at 32 C (708 243). Eggs incubated experimentally had a lower mean hatch rate at 20 C (243). Holt et al. (1988) collected seatrout eggs in Texas in temperatures ranging from 22 C to 31 C (1750). Larvae and juveniles have been collected in temperatures of 5-36 C (47 354 549 581); preferred temperatures range from 20-33 C (20 708). Adults have been taken in temperatures from 5.0 to 34.9 C (255 543), but prefer temperatures between 15-27 C (363), seeking nearshore waters if the extremes are reached (430). Although Reid (581) considered this species eurythermal as well as euryhaline, temperature has been reported as a limiting factor causing spotted seatrout to seek deeper water when temperature drops in the fall (581).

Hildebrand and Cable (1825) recorded numbing of trout by cold weather, and major cold kills have occurred in Texas (1285 1825). Simmons (651) reported active feeding and movement between 4-33 C. Sudden drops in temperature caused by severe cold fronts can result in mass mortality (253 468 489 701 1285), but at Sanibel Island, Florida spotted seatrout is considered one of the species least affected by cold weather (836 1068). In the Indian River Lagoon, Gilmore et al. (236) found no spotted seatrout killed in a hypothermal mortality with a minimum temperature of 6 C. The winter fish kills of spotted seatrout reported by Gunter (253) and Gunter and Hildebrand (1815) in Texas and the Gulf of Mexico, are unlikely in south Florida because low water temperature rarely occur there (253 1815). Storey (836) and Storey and Gudger (1068) reported that spotted seatrout was one of the coastal species least affected by unusually cold water in Sanibel Island, Florida (836 1068). However, in the Everglades National Park some spotted seatrout were numb or dead following a sudden temperature drop from 20 C at high tide to 18 C at low tide in the winter of 1960 (1242). It seems that the shallow depth, less than 3 m, induced the sharp temperature drop. To escape low winter water temperature, spotted seatrout in central Florida waters, Cedar Key and Indian River Lagoon, move into the warm waters of rivers and deep streams, channels and depressions near grass flats, and occasionally offshore (701 1284). Some estuaries can become death traps during cold waves because the fish become numb before they can escape to warmer offshore waters (701). Once the fish is driven to deeper waters by falling temperatures, the fish will tend to overwinter there (1778).

High temperatures in the summer also may regulate spotted seatrout abundance in coastal waters. When waters are unusually warm, spotted seatrout are likely to seek colder waters in deeper areas (430). Generally, when temperature dropped below16 C or rose above 25 C most spotted seatrout left the shallow waters along the banks of tidal creeks, rivers, and sounds (430). Temperatures for spawning range between 20-30 C (47), with temperatures below 25 C terminated spawning in the Indian River lagoon (1058 1638).

The growth of spotted seatrout is temperature-dependent. Growth is slowed in the winter because of reduced metabolism and feeding (700). Following a cold wave in Everglades National Park, the catch of spotted seatrout dropped to low levels for 10 days, and most of the fish stomachs were empty (1242). Growth is greatest in the summer at Ft. Myers and Cedar Key (1288).

Salinity: The best hatch rates for experimentally incubated eggs have been reported to occur at 15-25 ppt and 19-38 ppt at 28 C (641 243 1638). These eggs had a significantly lower hatch rate at 5 ppt, and all eggs died at any temperature when the salinity was 45 ppt. Eggs at 5 ppt would also sink to the bottom which would probably increase mortality in the wild. A critical minimum (0 ppt) and a critical maximum (50 ppt) were found that corresponded to 0% embryo survival at 28oC (641). Salinity acclimation of parents may also affect salinity tolerance of eggs (243). Optimal salinity for larvae is reported as ranging from 20-35 ppt (20), and from 18 to 32 ppt in Tampa Bay (664 1276). In the Indian River Lagoon, at salinities below 14 ppt seatrout spawning stopped (1858).

The juveniles and adults appear to prefer lower salinities (751). Juveniles seem to prefer salinities ranging from 8 to 25 ppt (559). Catches have been made in waters with salinities ranging from 2 to 34.9 ppt (255 751 559). In Florida, adults have been collected in salinities ranging from 0 to 37ppt (354 581 664 701 1051).  Maximum sustained swimming speeds occurred at salinities of 20-25 ppt (for fish 174-438 mm TL), but were reduced above and below these salinities (752).  Spotted seatrout have been taken in waters with salinity ranging from 0.2 to 37 ppt (65 1). However, Tabb suggested that salinity below 5 ppt was "intolerable" and that larvae and juveniles unable to move to more saline waters during post-storm freshets may suffer mass mortality (701).

Simmons (1957) reported that no spawning occurred in the Laguna Madre, TX at salinities greater than 45 ppt (651). Loman (1978) reported highest catches from waters of 20 to 35 ppt (No.). Wohlschlag and Wakeman (1798) suggested that minimum salinity stress occurs at 20 ppt for spotted seatrout from South Texas tested at 28°C (82°F). They also suggested that "there may be no excess available energy beyond ecological maintenance requirements at salinities below 10 ppt or above 45 ppt (1798). Optimum salinity for eggs and larvae was reported as 28.1 ppt with 100% survival predicted from 18.6 to 37.5 ppt (708).

Spotted seatrout have been caught in Florida in salinities ranging from 0 to 37 ppt (354 664 701 1051 1893). The greatest abundance is in the range 15 to 35 ppt (701). Optimum salinity in Texas, based on maximum sustained swimming performance, was 20 ppt for 174-435 mm TL fish (1798). The fish had difficulty maintaining swimming speeds at salinities below 10 ppt and above 45 ppt. The optimum salinity for eggs and larvae was 28 ppt, and Taniguchi (708) reported 100% survival in the range 19 -38 ppt (708). Juveniles and adults have similar "salinity preferences" (708). Spotted seatrout is especially vulnerable to abrupt changes in salinity during high freshwater inflow following heavy rainfall (701). Five ppt is apparently the minimum salinity in which larvae and juveniles survive. Higman (1824) found a significant correlation between the sport catch of adult spotted seatrout in a particular year and the annual rainfall in the 3 previous years (1824).

Dissolved Oxygen: Based on DO, salinity, temperature, depth, submerged aquatic vegetation, and wetlands a coefficient of habitat suitability was assigned (1648). This index was used to assess and map the probable distribution of spotted seatrout in the Gulf of Mexico estuaries (1648). Minimum metabolic oxygen demand for spotted seatrout tested at 28 C was 210, 125, and 230 mg oxygen/kg/hr at 10, 20, and 30 ppt respectively (741). No reports relating dissolved oxygen to distribution or abundance have been published. However, Etzold and Christmas (202) reported spotted seatrout killed in oxygen depletion kills. Spotted seatrout larvae died in aquaculture ponds when dissolved oxygen dropped below 4 ppm (1684). The oxygen requirements of spotted seatrout depend partly upon water temperature and salinity. The optimum temperature and salinity at Port Aransas, Texas were 28 C and 20 ppt respectively (1798).

Turbidity: Spotted seatrout live in a wide range of turbidities in estuaries in the northern Gulf of Mexico (163). However, Pearson (543) suggested a preference by spotted seatrout for "less turbid" areas. Tabb and Manning (702) and Perret suggested that excessively turbid waters following hurricane Donna caused mortality in spotted seatrout by packing the gill chambers with suspended solids (549). The effect of turbidity on egg survival is not known (1697). A quantitative study to correlate turbidity and distributional abundance of spotted seatrout is required.

pH: No reports relating distribution or abundance of spotted seatrout to pH have been published.

Light/Photoperiod: Wholschlag found that seasonal effects on metabolism were triggered by changees in light regimes (2175).  He found a late summer and autumn depression of metabolic rate and growth of spotted seatrout from Texas.  He also noted general debilitation. However, he pointed out that Wohlschlag’s data were limited because summer and winter were not included (2158).

Pohling (1858) and Pohling and Fuiman (2087) reported that spotted seatrout larvae were most abundant when light availability was the lowest, and were more dependent on mechanoreception, a sensory mechanism not dependent on light.

nodes.title: Currents/Tides
nodes.body:
The species/movement mechanism matrix indicates that eggs and larvae are passively moved through inlets, while larvae also show active-vertical movement through inlets. Coastal and tidal currents are the transport mechanisms for eggs and larvae while larvae are also transported by storms, active swimming, and geostrophic currents (1646).

Rutherford (1278) reported that successful catches of spotted seatrout larvae occurred in Florida Bay when current speed was <131 cm/sec.  Holt and Holt (2208) stated that larvae were collected at an average current speed of 39.5 cm/sec during diurnal ties, and 59.5 cm/sec during semi-diurnal tides in Aransas Bay, Texas.

Jannke (354) showed that the greatest catches of spotted seatrout larvae in the Everglades National Park occurred at night on flood tide.  Perez-Argudin (1878) indicated that the movement of spotted seatrout was associated with tides; larvae in Boca del Carmen, Campeche showed higher density (larvae/100 m^3) at mid-water (2-4 m).  Flores Cato and Perez-Argudin (1659) noted that larval spotted seatrout and silver seatrout were the only species subjected to tidal forces on their passage through El Carmen inlet: these larvae were captured typically during daytime in an 8 month study at three stations (1659).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body:
Trophic Mode: carnivore (741).
Feeding (by life stage): Spotted seatrout are opportunistic, visual carnivores relying almost solely on free swimming organisms for food (741). Prey items change as spotted trout increase in size (255 543 651 700 1284 1883). It was suggested that in southeastern Louisiana the spotted seatrout food habits were correlated with food availability, and that fish seemed to be the most important food group in the Biloxi marsh area (1755).

Food Items: (by life stage) Larvae feed primarily on zooplankton, switching to mostly benthic invertebrates as small juveniles (98 792 1106). McMichael and Peters (1276) identified more than 40 types of prey in stomachs of larval and juvenile seatrout. Copepods were the dominant food items and occurred in 83% of the fish examined. Copepods were not found in fish >45 mm (1276). Fish and shrimp were found to be the two most important food groups in seatrout larger than 15 mm (1276). Juveniles have been found to consume planktonic schizopods, mysids, isopods, amphipods, caridean and penaeid shrimp, killifish, and anchovies (98 1633 1565 1664 700 1276 1284). Young adults prey on a mixture of invertebrates and fish changing almost exclusively to fish as adult fish (162 163). The diets of larger juveniles and adults is skewed to the consumption of shrimp in the warmer months, and fish in the cooler months when shrimp are no longer available (255 543).

Prey selection was examined in laboratory experiments with spotted seatrout 160-210 mm TL (1764). Spotted seatrout, in tanks without an accessible substrate for burrowing, fed exclusively on brown shrimp (Peneaus aztecus) and did not eat available juvenile spot (Leiostomus xanthurus).  However, in tanks with sand substrate some spot were eaten. Burrowing by shrimp into the substrate apparently reduced their availability to the predators. Prey ranged in size from 59 to 85 mm TL, and spotted seatrout selected shrimp and spot within the lower half of this range. In a separate feeding trial, spotted seatrout selected juvenile spot over juvenile pinfish (Lagodon rhomboides) (1764).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Gender: Sexes separate.
Repro Mode: external fertilization of eggs by males.

nodes.title: Domain
nodes.body:
Fertilization: Spotted seatrout are dioecious and fertilization is external.
Spawning Strategy: Protracted spawning season, starting as early as February and ceasing in October, but generally from March to October (255 293 354 468 543 581 664 1057 1276 1284 1647). In Tampa Bay, spawning occurs from February to October with a spring peak in April-May and a summer peak in July-August (1276). There is intensive spawning activity during the summer months (1058 1276). Recorded temperature range for spawning is 21 C to 30 C with 23 C suggested as the minimum temperature for successful spawning (78 461).

In Florida, spawning is essentially completed when temperatures reach 28.3 C (701 363). Peak spawning occurs between 30-35 ppt, and it is suspected that lower salinities may reduce survival (701), or terminate spawning (1058). No spawning has been observed above 45 ppt (651). Spawning occurs primarily within coastal bays and lagoons, usually in deeper holes or channels with the eggs drifting into the grassy areas or in shallow grassy areas (468 543 762 1285 1058). Some evidence indicates that spawning may also occur in tidal passes, in areas of little or no vegetation, and in low to medium salinity in nearshore waters of the Gulf of Mexico (614 9).

Spawning probably occurs in estuarine waters 3-4.6 m deep (543 701 202), within grass beds or near passes. It is carried out at night (748). But, also occurred at dusk ( ), and in Tampa Bay on or near the full moon (78 549 1276). Spawning peaks appeared to coincide with increasing or decreasing photoperiods (293) and it was related to water temperature (78 549). Spotted seatrout spawn near dusk in the Indian River Lagoon (1909). Fresh postovulatory follicles along with ovulated eggs were found between 1800 and 2100 hrs, just after ovulation had occurred (1909). Brown-Petterson et al. (1736) also reported that spotted seatrout spawn during a 2-hour period near dusk (78 1736). The final stages of oocyte maturation appear to require 6-8 hrs for completion in Indian River Lagoon (1909) and 10 hours in Texas (78 1736).

Reproductive Periodicity: A close relationship between spawning season and water temperature was reported from a comparison between temperate Chesapeake Bay, Virginia and subtropical Port Aransas, Texas (1736). Females spawn once or twice in Virginia but multiple times in Texas (1736). Spawning frequency was high in Texas, where it was estimated to occur every 2.3 to 3.6 days or 50 times per season in shallow bays (78). This frequency is probably not sustained throughout the entire spawning season (78). Other estimates suggested that females spawned in captivity in Indian River, Florida three times every 16 to 21 days (1291).

Spawning frequency varies with age, and older fish spawn more frequently than younger fish (1 909). In the Indian River Lagoon female spotted seatrout spawn about every 3-4 days (1909). Based on an April 1 to September season (183 days), an average seatrout would spawn 56.3 times in a season (1909). Older spotted seatrout contribute disproportionately to total egg production because they spawn more frequently than younger fish (1909). The spawning season extended from May to mid-August in Virginia and from April to the end of September in Texas (1736). Chiefly in April and May off the North Carolina coast (1825).

Florida: Spawning occurred in the Cedar Key area, from late March or early April to October (1284), and from Cedar Key to Ft. Myers, from late March to September, peaking in June-August (1284 1288). In Indian River Lagoon, spawning occurred from mid-April to late July, peaking in April-June (700). Spawning is most intense during May-August in the Indian River Lagoon (1909). Everglades National Park, year round, peaking in late summer/fall (1242, 354, 1435). Tampa Bay, from February to October, spring peak in April-May, summer peak July-August (1276). Data for Charlotte Harbor, Florida Bay and Jacksonville are not available.

The time of spawning is controlled largely by temperature and salinity. In Everglades National Park, Stewart (1242) correlated spawning peaks with water temperatures between 28 C and 30 C, and Jannke (354) found that temperatures above 30 C reduced the intensity of spring spawning. In south Florida, the fish spawned when water temperatures reached 25 C but ceased if temperature reached 28 C (1778). Spawning usually peaked in the spring when salinity was 30 - 35 ppt. According to Tabb (701) spawning occurs at night. Spawning is suspected to take place in tidal streams, or above tidal influence (543; 701). There is evidence that spawning takes place in the tidal areas (701), in open bays (1825), near barrier islands (549; 402), or outside estuaries (702). Based on histological and other evidence, most fish in Mississippi apparently spawned periodically from April to September and even longer in years with appropriate temperature conditions (1769).

Parental Care: None.
Seasonal energetics: No information available (549).

nodes.title: Maturation
nodes.body:
Males mature as early as their first year and females by the end of the second year (383 700). Some females mature as early as 231 mm and >90% reach sexual maturity at 271 mm SL in Texas and all females are mature by 300 mm SL (78). Males are much smaller than females at maturity with all fish 200 mm SL (the smallest size collected) and over being mature (78).  Maturity and spawning first occur at 2 years of age (543).

Klima and Tabb (383) reported that all females in Apalachicola Bay, Florida, were mature at 270 mm SL and all males at 250 mm; the lengths of the smallest ripe female and male were 210 and 180 mm SL respectively. Stewart (1242) reported that most fish in Florida Bay matured at 190-300 mm SL with no difference between sexes. Tabb (1961) reported that spotted seatrout matured at larger sizes along the Atlantic coast of Florida than those along the Gulf coast. Most females matured at lengths greater than 350 mm SL in the Indian River Lagoon, Florida.

In Chesapeake Bay 20% of two-year old females had maturing gonads but all males were sexually mature in their second year (1735). The GSI indicated that females had two spawning peaks (May 18 to June 14, and July 13 to July 24), while males had only one peak (May 18 to June 28) (1735). Females matured at 267 mm SL in Virginia and 232 mm SL in Texas. All males collected in both areas were sexually mature. The smallest male was 221 mm SL in Virginia and 196 mm SL in Texas (1736). Fish vary in size at maturity from estuary to estuary (549). Pearson found that in Texas spotted seatrout matured at the end of the second year but did not spawn until the third (543). Females matured as short as 189 mm SL and males by 201 mm in Mississippi during 1983 (1769). By the time fish reached 40 cm, females constituted 85.7% of the sample from Mississippi Sound, not counting additional samples in 1982 than contained more males between 350-475 mm than females (1769). Sexually mature fish tended to group in schools composed primarily of females or males (1769).

Some seatrout spawn at age 0 in the Indian River Lagoon (1909). Crabtree and Adams (1903) found 43 Y-O-Y, ranging from 237 to 480 mm, with either hydrated oocytes or fresh postovulatory follicles. Plasma vitellogenin was measured by homologous radioimmunoassay. Vitellogenin was purified from plasma of estrogen-treated fish and was shown to be a protein of approximately 200,000 d of molecular weight. Antisera were raised against the isolated protein and a radioimmunoassay (RIA) was developed.

The substance measured with RIA was female-specific, hepatically derived, estrogen-inducible, and immunologically related to oocyte yolk proteins. Vitellogenin levels in the plasma of female spotted seatrout were shown to rise dramatically during the period of ovarian recrudescence (1742).  Maturational gonadotropin (GTH) subunits were isolated from pituitaries by ethanol extraction, ion-exchange, gel-filtration, and reverse-phase chromatography. Partial amino acid sequencing of the N-terminal regions of the alpha and beta subunits indicated 60-80% identity with various carp and salmon GTH subunits. The spotted seatrout GTH beta subunit was used as radioligand in a RIA with Atlantic croaker (Micropogonias undulatus) GTH antiserum. Pituitary extracts and plasmas from a variety of sciaenid fishes diluted parallel to the croaker suggesting a high degree of immunological similarity among the GTH beta subunits (1653).  Patino and Thomas (1990) characterized the binding activity of radioactive 17a, 20P-21-trihydroxy-4-pregnen-3-one (20P-S) to plasma membranes from the ovaries of spotted seatrout. The results suggested that the 20P-S activity represent authentic maturation inducing substance (MIS) of spotted seatrout (1680). A progestogen receptor involved in final oocyte maturation, hydration, and ovulation was characterized (1681 1682).

Fecundity: Spotted seatrout are multiple spawners and their fecundity is difficult to accurately determine (78). Estimates of fecundity range from a mean of 14,000 from 283 mm TL year-I class females to 1.1 million eggs for IV-year class averaging 504 mm TL (688). Summaries of fecundity at various sizes are presented by several authors (363 461 792). Recent evidence suggests that these fecundity estimates may be low and that actual annual fecundity may average greater than 10 million eggs (78). Generally, fecundity increases with age and size. Ovaries contained more oocytes in fish from Mississippi than indicated in the literature. The largest estimate of oocytes over 30 pm in diameter per female was 10.5 x 10^6 using a volumetric displacement method, or 15.5 x 10^6 when calculated using a gravimetric technique (1769). Estimates of total annual egg production range from 7 to 52 million in the Indian River Lagoon (1909). Batch fecundity was estimated for 82 fish and ranged from 7,493 to 797,515 oocytes (1909).

Development (by life stage): The SST egg is spherical and usually contains an oil droplet. Egg diameter ranges between 0.7-0.85 mm; hatch occurs 16 to 20 hours after fertilization at 25oC (204). Larvae hatch at a length of about 1.7 mm (363 1637).  In the laboratory, larvae grew at 25oC from 1.5 rnm SL at hatching to 4.5 mm SL in 15 days (204 1637).

nodes.title: Mating/Spawning
nodes.body: Sex Ratio: Several studies have reported a preponderance of males among younger year classes, a near 1:1 ratio at age II to III, and all or nearly all females by age V to VI or older (383 700 1288). This shift is attributed to greater longevity of female fish. Susceptibility to capture and distributional segregation among juveniles is not mentioned (402).

nodes.title: GROWTH
nodes.body:
Length Range: (by life stage)
Larval stage sizes range from ca. 1.8 to 10-12 mm TL (363).
Juveniles range from 10-12 to 180-200 mm TL (363).
Adult: Maximum size is reported as 910 mm (788) to 1250 mm (327) and 7.0 kg (788).

Length Conversions: The standard length (SL) - total length (TL) relationship for 9,857 fish ranging 36-744 mm SL was:

TL (mm) = 11.804 + 1.138 SL (mm), r = 0.997 (1717).

nodes.title: Weight Conversions
nodes.body:
The dressed weight (DW) - whole weight (WW) relationship for 617 fish ranging 0.305 - 4.595 kg of DW was:

WW (kg) = -33.338 + 1.151 DW (g), r = 0.995 (1717).

nodes.title: Wet-Dry Weight Conversions
nodes.body:
Weight-Length Relationship: Length-weight equations for adult seatrout from Everglades National Park calculated by Rutherford (1278) are presented in Johnson and Seaman (792). Males mature as early as their first year and females by the end of the second year (383 700). Some females mature as early as 231 mm and >90% reach sexual maturity at 271 mm SL in Texas and all females are mature by 300 mm SL (78). Males are much smaller than females at maturity with all fish 200 mm SL (the smallest size collected) and over being mature (78).  Maturity and spawning first occur at 2 years of age (543). Maximum size is reported as 910 mm (788) to 1250 mm (327) and 7.0 kg (788).

Length at Age: (male/female/both):
Larvae and juveniles: McMichael and Peters (1276) used otolith daily growth ring counts for the determination of age and growth of larvae collected in Tampa Bay. They provided the following equations for size-at-age and age-at-size for seatrout smaller than 50mm:

 	L=0.509(A),    r^2 = 0.96
 	A=2.476(L) - 0.012(L)^2,      r^2=0.96

where: L=notochord or standard length in mm and A=age in days.

Using these equations they calculated that a 7.0 mm larva would be about 17 d old, a 25 mm juvenile to average 54 d old, and a 50 mm juvenile would be about 94 d old (1276).

Adults: Age-length frequency data based on scale analysis have been presented for Punta Gorda, FL (76), Fort Myers (1288), Cedar Key (1288), Everglades National Park (1292), northwest Florida (383), and Corpus Christ, TX (543). These data are presented in tabular form by Johnson (363) and graphically by Johnson and Seaman (792). In general, seatrout from the Florida Atlantic coast are larger at a given age than those occurring elsewhere. Yearly growth rates of seatrout vary with geographic location and are probably governed by temperature, habitat, salinity, and/or other factors (549).

Longevity: Adults can live up to 15 years (461).

Aging Structures/Methods: Estimates of age and growth were done analyzing fish from commercial and recreational catches in 1986-1988 in three Florida estuaries: Apalachicola Bay, Charlotte Harbor, and Indian River Lagoon (1678). Thin otolith, sagittae were used to determine age; annulus formation occurred in November-May. Spotted seatrout reached 301-327 mm TL at the end of their first year. Females were generally larger than males, although growth was highly variable. After age 1, male growth slowed to an average of 34-5 1 mm/year and was modeled best by area-specific Gompertz growth equations. Males and females from Indian River Lagoon and Apalachicola Bay were generally larger than those from Charlotte Harbor. Males were heavier than females of the same length. Patterns of growth did not reflect those previously used to support hypothesized divisions of spotted seatrout into separate subpopulations in Florida estuaries. Differences in growth and age composition observed among estuaries may reflect differences in environmental and fishing effects rather than genetic differentiation among estuaries (1678).  A comparison between Naples Bay and Fakahatchee Bay in Florida found a spotted seatrout larval growth rate of 0.4 mm/day for both areas (1277).

Age and growth in the Indian River Lagoon were estimated from scales and sectioned otoliths for 184 specimens collected between November 1986 and April 1988. Marginal increment measurements showed that a single annulus formed on scales and otoliths during March and April.  The otolith method was more reliable and it was the preferred method for estimating growth in this study. The Von Bertalanffy growth equation seemed to accurately describe growth in the Indian River Lagoon up to age class five. Back-calculated growth rates from otoliths were similar to those estimated 30 years ago. Data indicated that average back-calculated standard length at age class estimated by the Florida Marine Research Institute did not agree with those found in this study. It was assumed that these differences were due to the different methods used to derive these data. It was suggested that length at age was underestimated by both methods (1652).

Estimates of age and growth from sectioned otoliths for 425 fish collected in Galveston Bay, Texas indicated: 1. A single annulus was formed between March-April; 2. Annulus counts made independently by two readers agreed completely, suggesting that age interpretation was precise; 3. After age 1, back-calculated length-at-age estimates were much greater for females than males; 4. Spotted seatrout grew faster in Galveston Bay than fish collected from other areas in the Gulf; 5.Gonodo-Somatic Index (GSI) values, measured as the gonad weight:body weight ratio, reflected a 6-month spawning period. This may account for a four-fold difference in back-calculated length at age I; 6. The length advantage gained by larger individuals at age I was maintained as they grew older (1757, 1758).

nodes.title: Growth Equations
nodes.body:
Pearson (543) stated that little increment in size appeared from November to March, but in early spring growth resumed and annuli were formed in the scales. Apparently females have a higher growth rate than males (202 543). Back-calculation is the method preferred to determine growth rate instead of length-frequency distribution because of the protracted spawning season causes overlap between size classes (402).

Larval age and growth equations for seatrout collected in Naples and Fakahatchee Bays in southwest Florida were:

 	 I=2.326(L) + 0.181, r^2=0.94
 	 L=0.405(I) + 0.116, r^2=0.94,

where: I = daily otolith increment number (i.e. age in days), and L = standard length in mm (1277).

The growth rates in Tampa Bay and Naples/Fakahatchee Bays were similar and approximated 0.4 mm/day (1276 1277).

The following equations were derived to describe growth of Tampa Bay seatrout between 10 and 170 mm (1276):

 	 L=0.448(A) + 0.002(A)^2,        r^2=0.86
 	A=12.472 + 1.836(L) - 0.005(L)^2,               r^2=0.88

These equations predict that a 25 mm juvenile will average 55 d old, and a 50 mm juvenile, 92 d old. The largest juveniles collected (170 mm) averaged about 6.5 mo old. Juveniles exhibited growth rates of 13 to 18 mm/mo during the fall (1 276).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: Commercial landings occur throughout the year in the Gulf of Mexico. Landings data since 1964 indicate a concentrated fishery in western Florida, Louisiana, and Texas; east coast landings are minor by comparison (1282). Fresh catch is sold in local markets (791). Runaround gill nets, trammel nets and longlines are the common gear used (461 791). Most trout are caught incidentally while fishing for other inshore fishes (402 549). Florida landings for 1989 amounted to 1,143,329 lbs worth $1,239,129 ($1.08/lb), with west coast landings accounting for 815,827 lbs (902). A downward trend in Florida landings has been evident since the mid-1960's; landings have declined from 4.8 million lbs in 1952 to 2.5 million lbs in 1982 (792 1282). Commercial landings of spotted seatrout in the Sarasota Bay area have declined from 430,000 lbs in 1951 to less than 100,000 lbs annually in the 1980's (1274). Spotted seatrout are classified as a restricted species (Department of Environmental Protection-DEP).

Recreational: Sport catch is substantially greater than commercial. Fishery information for the Gulf of Mexico showed a total catch of 20,360,000 spotted seatrout in 1988 (5 13). Seatrout are taken on light to heavy spinning tackle from shorelines, piers and boats in nearshore Gulf waters, inshore estuarine bays, sounds, bayous and tidal streams (402 549). A survey conducted from 1972-1977 in Everglades National park found that seatrout was the first or second choice of sport fishermen in 4 of the 5 survey years (1275). A creel census conducted in Sarasota Bay in 1991 indicated that seatrout was the most sought-after species and was the primary target in 71% of the cases where a target species was mentioned by sport fishermen (1274). Currently, the recreational bag limit is 10 fish per day; with each fish being not less than 14 inches or greater than 24 inches. One fish over 24 inches is allowed (DEP).

The effect of size limit upon the harvest was determined through comparisons of lengths and weights collected before (1977-1978) and after (1979-1981) the regulation went into effect in Texas. The percentage of sublegal, 300 mm SL, fish landed was significantly different among bays and significantly smaller after the regulation was in effect. The overall decrease in the percentage of sublegal fish that was landed indicated that most of the anglers were complying with the size limit. A significant change was found in the mean weight of the catch from one bay after the size limit was established. However, mean weight data were insensitive for determining the effects of the regulation. The size limit affected the recreational harvest by 1. Decreasing the number of spotted seatrout 300 mm or shorter that were creeled, and 2. Increasing the number of spotted seatrout available for spawning (1766).

nodes.title: Ecological Role
nodes.body:
Perret et a1 (549) referred to the spotted seatrout as an opportunistic carnivore whose food changes with size. The pattern of change in diet is typically found in fish inhabiting areas with abundant seagrass coverage, e.g., Florida and Texas, but may differ in areas with lower abundance of seagrass, e.g., Lake Pontchartrain, Louisiana (Darnell, 1958). Feeding habits between stages may be different, but feeding within stages is apparently non-selective (700). Moody (1284) attributed the high percentage (54%) of empty guts founds in his study to sporadic feeding, and Darnel1 (163) suggested that the feeding was heaviest during the early to mid-morning hours. The role of spotted seatrout in estuarine trophic dynamics is.. .??

Species Stress: A major long-term decline in commercial catches may be due in part to loss of seagrass habitat in Tampa Bay (1679). The influence of reduced salinity, capture, handling, and transportation was evaluated by measuring levels of zinc associated proteins of the liver or metallothionein-like (MT) proteins (1639). A significant increase in MT proteins was observed. The increase of MT proteins level has also been observed in females collected during the reproductive season compared to regressed females (1639). Three MT proteins from oocytes and developing eggs were identified by gel filtration analysis (1640 1641).

nodes.title: STOCK ENHANCEMENT
nodes.body:
Induced Breeding: Spotted seatrout spawned during each of 13 consecutive months under a light regime of 15 h light-9 h dark and 26 C temperature (20). Strip-spawning trials were performed after females received injections of 250, 500, and 1,100 IU human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG)/kg of body weight (BW), and 10, 50, and 100 mg of carp pituitary extract/kg BW; 10, 50, and 100 mg of salmon pituitary extract/kg BW, and a crude spotted seatrout pituitary extract administered as two, four, or six pituitaries per fish. All the hormones induced ovulation and there was not a significant difference in fertilization (P>0.05) (1650).

A sex-steroid binding protein (SBP) that binds both testosterone and estradiol-17P was identified in plasma and ovarian interstitial fluids. This SBP has a high affinity for a range of estrogens and androgens. It molecular mass was estimated as 135 kDa. Its activity was destroyed by exposure to EDTA, dithiothreitol (DTT), or temperature above 50°C (1668). The purified protein was dissociated into two identical subunits with mass of 49 to 52 kDa. Its N-terminal sequence and amino acid composition were not similar to mammalian SBP. The plasma levels of this protein increased in association with ovarian recrudescence suggesting a role in reproductive physiology. This SPB binds to several "environmental estrogens" including o,p'-DDE, methoxychlor, and PCBs (1669).

Rearing: Methods and techniques for rearing spotted seatrout in the laboratory have been described (20). Egg and early larval development have been described (1637). Salinity and temperature tolerance limits for larval stage were evaluated (1638). The eggs hatched after 18 h (20). Age-related changes in salinity tolerance of larval spotted seatrout were evaluated (1643). This study indicated that parental and/or early acclimation effects are important in early development (up to 9 days) (1643).

Medial lethal concentrations (LC50) of ammonia and nitrite were determined in static tests for eggs, larvae hatched from eggs previously exposed, larvae hatched from eggs not exposed, one month old juveniles, and four-month old juveniles. The egg was the life history stage most tolerant to unionized ammonia. 91.6% hatch occurred at 6.0 mg NH3-NIL. The 24 h LC50 for larvae hatched from both ammonia-exposed and unexposed eggs was 0.28 mg NH3-NIL (1743).

Feeding: Newly hatched seatrout were fed rotifers (Brachionis plicatilis) and brine shrimp (Artemia sp.) (20). Larval spotted seatrout grew faster on 1 and 2 day pre-fed brine shrimp (Artemia salina) nauplii than fish fed newly hatched nauplii. One day old brine shrimp nauplii are a better food organism for spotted seatrout12 to 21 days of age than newly hatched nauplii because of their bigger size (1761).

The effect of artificial Spartina structure on predation rates of spotted seatrout was examined in laboratory conditions. Vegetative structure reduced predation rates of spotted seatrout on brown shrimp (Penaeus aztecus), and spotted seatrout appeared to be a visual feeder (1763).

Stocking: Pond culture trials on the central coast of Texas were used to examine 38 independent variables associated with stocking density, length of the culture period, fertilization, water quality, zooplankton densities on percent harvest, number of fish harvest/ha, and kg of fish harvested/ha/day of culture (1649). The stepwise multiple regression analysis of the observed variation in kg of fish harvested/ha/day of culture was best explained by mean temperature, stocking density, and mean polychaete larvae densities in the first and fourth week after stocking. During the latter stages of culture, from larvae to fingerlings up to 30 mm TL, polychaete larvae density was the most important factor (1649).

A comparison between 3 fertilized saltwater ponds, 0.1 ha, and 3 identical ponds receiving a supplement of 4 billion brine shrimp nauplii/ha was performed. No brine shrimp were recovered in biweekly zooplankton samples or fingerling stomachs, and no significant differences for growth, survival, or production between treatments were observed. After 22 days, mean total length, weight, and percent recovery of fingerlings from the six ponds was 39 +/- 2 mm, 0.58 ± 0.10 g, and 8.4 +/- 2.2%. Average production was 46.9 +/-7.2 kg/ha and 2.1 +/- 0.3 kg/ha/day (1771).

A morphometric comparison of fingerling spotted seatrout, orangemouth corvina, Cynoscion xanthurus, and their hybrids was done (1 772). The initial analysis yielded a discriminant function which correctly classified 95% of the fish. All data were used to provide a new discriminant function which correctly classified 90.8% of the fish. Therefore, morphometric analysis could be used to distinguish between parents and both hybrids where fingerlings are stocked together (1772).

In response to stock identification and hatchery-product evaluation concerns, the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department conducted extensive genetic surveys to estimate levels of genetic variation, to delineate population structure, and to identify rare alleles that could be use as genetic markers (1666). Allozyme analyses suggested that spotted seatrout in the areas surveyed are single, randomly mating populations. Rare alleles appear to be inherited according to Mendel's single expectations, and no differences in growth were observed among fish of various ages possessing all possible marker allele genotypes
(1666). Significant clinical variation was observed at the aspartate aminotransferase-2 locus, and in average individual heterozygosity. The genetic survey led to modifications of the stocking program, i.e., clinical variation resulted in three distinct broodstocks representative of the upper, middle, and lower Texas coast (1666).

nodes.title: POPULATION
nodes.body: Stock Assessment (discuss parameters for each assessment):

nodes.title: Total Mortality
nodes.body:
Natural Mortality: Analysis of the stomach contents of 38 bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) stranded between 1976- 1992 in the Indian River Lagoon System (IRL) were examined. Spotted seatrout was the most common fish found in the stomachs. Assuming a hypothetical population of 400 dolphins year-round residents in the IRL, dolphins consumed 790 m tons of fish per year (1770).

Annual mortality for all fish was 77% in the Everglades National Park for Nov 1978 to Jan 1980 (1775). Males had higher annual mortality and conditional fishing mortality than females. Conditional natural mortality was the same for both sexes. Mortality was different than that observed in 1961 (1242).

The apparent larval instantaneous daily mortality coefficient was significantly larger in Naples Bay, 0.64, than in Fakahatchee Bay, 0.36, P< 0.001 (1277).

nodes.title: Fishing Mortality
nodes.body:
Sport fishing intensity for spotted seatrout in the Everglades National Park is highest during cold winter when the fish congregate in deep holes and channels and are more available to the fishermen (1824).

To reduce the bycatch of spotted seatrout in Texas commercial trotline, hook placement within the water column was examined. The commercial trotline was simulated in the Laguna Madre during February 1985 through 1986. Placement of the trotline hooks on bottom will reduce bycatch of spotted seatrout and other non-marketable fishes and improve operational efficiency of commercial fishermen without significantly reducing catch of black drum, the target species (1759). Muoneke and Childress (1675) reviewed the recreational fishery in Texas (1675). Catch and release (hooking) mortality, was reviewed from literature and from a survey of fisheries management agencies in all 50 states. Most hooking mortalities occurred within 24 hrs; the use of initial plus delayed mortality provided a more complete estimate of mortality. Single hooks resulted in higher mortality than with treble hooks. Environmental conditions, notably high water temperature and low dissolved oxygen, are important to overall mortality related to hooking, playing, and handling. Mortalities were highly variable. It was about 68% in spotted seatrout. The many variables potentially affecting hooking mortality may make optimal management of particular species and water bodies difficult using regional-level or statewide management regulations (1675).

The short-term, 48 hrs, post-release mortality of spotted seatrout caught in "run-around" gill nets, or by hook and line in Tampa Bay, Florida were investigated during October 1991 to February 1993 (1676). Overall mortality of spotted seatrout caught by and release from hook and line was 4.6% and was influenced by hooking location. More than 25% of gut-hooked fish died after release, whereas less than 2% of fish hooked in the eye, gill arch, jaws, or inside the mouth died. Overall mortality of fish captured in gill nets was 28% and was influenced significantly by water temperature. Mean mortalities were 10-40% at water temperatures of 16-23 C, and 47-69% at 28-31C. Fish captured in gill nets were more likely to die after release than were fish caught by hook and line. The number of spotted seatrout that died in Florida during 1992 after release from gill nets was about two orders of magnitude less than the number that died after release from hook and line. Under high levels of fishing effort, the mortality of released fish may substantially reduce the benefits of creel or harvest restrictions (1676).

Abundance by Month:

Abundance by Year:

Population Abundance: A von Bertalanffy growth curve, L = 65.47 cm (1 - e super (-0.2005(t + 0.41 13 yr))), was derived for published data in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico to construct a yield per-recruit contour. Maximum yield-per-recruit is approached as F increases above 1 and age of first entry approaches 3.9 years (14.9 in, 1.1 lb). A linear regression is derived relating average size of capture to gill net mesh size (MS in inches). L = 1.97 + 8.63 MS, and used along with legal sizes of first harvest to evaluate the impact of current laws in the Gulf states on yield-per-recruit (1741).

Analysis of relative abundance estimates and utilization of estuaries indicate that spotted seatrout makes moderate to high utilization of estuaries and inlets from Cape Fear, North Carolina southward to Angelfish Creek in Florida (1671).

The abundance of spotted seatrout in ichthyoplankton samples offshore of Fourleague Bay, Louisiana was estimated between Nov 1987 and Jan 1990 (1523). Spotted seatrout was associated with bay anchovy, Anchoa mitchilli, naked goby, Microgobius sp., and skillet fish, Gobiesox strumosus. These species were the most abundant in warm water, >23oC, along a transect from offshore to Oyster Bayou tidal pass. The analysis showed that spotted seatrout and all the other species were more abundant on flood than ebb tides, and larval densities were often statistically greater near the bottom, suggesting tidal transport and/or retention (1523).

nodes.title: Management Regulations
nodes.body:
Management measures in 1984 included a minimum size limit of 12 inches TL with comparable mesh size regulations in directed fisheries, and data collection for stock assessment and to monitor the status of the fisheries (where?, what state?). High priority for research included stock identification, mortality estimates and yield modeling, habitat requirements, effects of environmental factors on stock size, development of a pre-recruit index, mesh size selectivity, and social and economic analyses (1762).

It has been suggested to use age-specific differences in spawning frequencies to estimate both spawning potential ratio and total egg production (1909).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
A brief summary of the ecology of the spotted seatrout, and other sciaenids, was reported by Darovec (1744).

Competition: Spotted seatrout may be the only abundant large carnivore in some estuaries (701). Probable competitors for food and space in the early planktivore stage are larvae of other sciaenids, pinfish, hardhead catfish, juveniles of menhaden, anchovies, and silversides, adult menhaden and anchovies (163). In addition, invertebrate larvae and adults of crustaceans, coelenterates, molluscs, ctenophores, and polychaetes may also compete for food with larval spotted seatrout. The adult spotted seatrout compete with those species that also feed on shrimp and fish such as sand trout (Cynoscion arenarius), redfish (Sciaenops ocellatus), flounder, saltwater catfishes, gar, snook, snappers, jacks, and tarpon (Megalops atlanticus). According to Darnell (163) spotted seatrout, silver perch (Bairdiella chrysura), and tarpon of similar lengths have similar food habits. The potential impact of the spotted seatrout as an estuarine predator might be surmised from studies of community-level interactions for a power plant cooling lake in upper Galveston Bay, Texas (Johnson, 1982). During 1972-1979, the abundance of various prey (white shrimp, brown shrimp, blue crabs, menhaden, croaker, anchovies, and silversides) was inversely related to the abundance of predatory fishes, of which spotted seatrout and sand seatrout comprised 90%.

Predation: Analysis of the stomach contents of 38 bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) stranded between 1976-1992 in the Indian River Lagoon System (IRL) were examined. Spotted seatrout was the most common fish found in the stomachs. Assuming a hypothetical population of 400 dolphins year-round residents in the IRL, dolphins consumed 790 m tons of fish per year (1770). Interspecific competition is common at all stages of the life cycle, and the susceptibility of spotted seatrout to predation by other piscivorous species is greatest among larvae and juveniles. Spotted seatrout is second only to sea catfish and mullet in the diet of Florida Bay osprey (Tabb personal communication reference?).

nodes.title: Parasites/Diseases
nodes.body:
Lorio and Perret (1281) briefly reviewed parasites and diseases in spotted seatrout. Most parasites are not harmful to man, but they alter growth pattern and cause scarring in the fish themselves (543).

The infections caused by plerocercoids of the cestode Poecilancistrium caryophyllum
(Trypanorhyncha) primarily involved the middle of a fillet or the region adjacent to the vertebral column below the dorsal fins. This worm causes an esthetically displeasing product and consequently depressed the value of the fishery (1768 1769). However, these worms do not affect the taste of the fish and are not infectious to humans (Parker, 1951, Chandler, 1954). Sampling of the commercial catch during Aug-Oct, 1982 at Steinhatchee, Florida, 60 miles north of Seahorse Key in the Gulf of Mexico, showed 81.9% of the fish were infected (1739). The maximum infection intensity was 10 plerocercoids per fish with a mean = 2.65. There was a correlation between intensity and fish length. The condition coefficient (K) and intensity were negatively correlated (1739). According to Overstreet (1977) based on K and liver-weight analysis there is no evidence for mortality due to infection of P. caryophyllum nor heavily infected hosts are being prayed upon because they are apparently debilitated (1768 1769). In over 3,000 sciaenid fish examined in Mississippi Sound, 40% of the spotted seatrout possessed an average of 2 worms per fish, which was comparable with fish from Texas, Louisiana, and Tampa Bay. However, values were twice as high in Apalachee Bay (1768). Seasonal sampling in Mississippi Sound indicated fluctuations but not clear-cut trends. It is suspected that infection is related with salinity fluctuations (1768). The prevalence of infections increases as the fish increases in length, but not the intensity suggesting an immune response (1768). No fish less than 140 mm SL and relatively few less than 250 mm SL had infections,  suggesting either the unavailability of the intermediate host to young fish or the ultimate death of most young infected fish (1768). Relatively more male than female fish harbored parasites, but the significance of this finding is questioned (1768).

The copepod Lernanthropus gisleri is the most common ectoparasite on the gills of spotted seatrout from Florida, Louisiana, Texas, and Mexico (1285).  The spotted seatrout is also host of the following flatworms (Monogenea; Platyhelminthes) parasites: Diplectanum bilobatum Hargis, 1955 (Diplectanidae), Neoheterobothrium cynoscioni (MacCallum, 1917) (Diclidophoridae); Cynoscionicola heteracantha (Manter, 1938) (Microcotylidae) (Hendrix, 1994).

nodes.title: Eutrophication
nodes.body: Pollutant Toxicity: Bryan (80) found levels of DDT in the ovaries and eggs to be 4.77 and 2.93 ppm, respectively, and considered these concentrations to affect the reproductive capacity of spotted seatrout in the lower Laguna Madre, Texas. However, Butler (87) indicates that successful spawning can occur with concentrations as high as 8 ppm in the ovaries. See (361 362). Also see (1697, 361, 1807, 362)

nodes.title: Entrainment/Impingement
nodes.body:
Perturbations: The importance of estuaries to the spotted seatrout was emphasized by Etzold and Christmas (1979). Most studies have suggested that seagrass beds are the preferred habitat of postlarvae, juveniles, and adults (543, 1284, 701). However, spotted seatrout may occur abundantly near areas without extensive seagrass beds, e.g., shell reefs, marshes, and submerged or emergent islands (1281). Perret et a1. (549) seem to correlate distribution more with food abundance. Tabb (1778) suggested that several ecological characteristics were important in determining the abundance of spotted seatrout in Indian River, Florida: 1. Large areas of shallow, quiet brackish water; 2. Extensive seagrass beds usually dominated by Thalassia testudinum and Halodule wrightii; 3. Deep water areas adjacent to seagrass beds, 3 to 6 m, to be used as refuge in the winter; 4. Abundant food supply; 5. Absence of predators - not identified; 6. Absence of competitors - not identified; 7. Temperature between 15 and 27°C. The effects of severe ecological changes on the utilization of Florida Bay as a gamefish nursery were studied. The distribution, relative abundance, and size structure of juvenile gamefish were collectively analyzed and compared to the results of similar historical surveys prior to the perturbations. Many species important to Florida Bay recreational fishery, e.g., common snook, red drum, sheepshead, and bonefish have been absent or extremely rare indicating that major portions of Florida Bay never served as a significant nursery area for these species. But, spotted seatrout and gray snapper appear to utilize Florida Bay as a nursery area. These species have showed different responses to the recent habitat changes. Spotted seatrout juveniles currently have higher densities and a wider distribution than had been observed earlier, including an expansion of the nursery area into some of the most heavily impacted regions, while grey snapper appear to have declined slightly and its present distribution may be more restricted than in the past (1651).

The changes in Florida Bay larval fish community in response to seagrass die-off and the restoration efforts were analyzed (1683). The abundance and distribution of larval fish prior to the seagrass die-off, 1984-1985, to the present, 1994- 1995, were compared. Spotted seatrout was of particular interest because it spends its entire life in estuarine waters. From past and present sampling it was found that spotted seatrout spawn: 1. in the western portion of Florida Bay adjacent to the mainland from Cape Sable to Crocodile Point and waters where salinity is higher than 20 ppt; 2. along the edge of the Gulf of Mexico; 3. in a portion of the central and western interior.  Spawning does not appear to occur in water adjacent to the Keys, in eastern Florida Bay adjacent to the mainland, or in water where salinity is 120 ppt (1683).

nodes.title: Climate
nodes.body:
Other: A comprehensive understanding at a larger scale is essential to implement any management program (1904). Focus on the larger system provides an adequate scale to review the ecological history, natural catastrophic events, and human impacts that influence the dynamic relationships between subsystems. Darnel1 (1904) reviewed literature pertinent to the Alabama/Mississippi continental shelf and associated coastal waters. This complex ecological system is subject to episodic catastrophic events like: 1. cold fronts; 2. Floods; 3. major storms and hurricanes; 4. hypoxic events; and 5. red tide outbreaks. These events should be considered at a larger scale.

Hypoxic events: The area of low dissolved oxygen of the Louisiana coast was large in 1998, but it does not rival the extensive areas mapped in the five years since the 1993 flood of the Mississippi River according to preliminary estimates of Dr. N. Rabalais, LUMCON. The "dead zone" was mapped on a seven-day cruise in late July. It measured 4,800 square miles, and it was concentrated on the eastern and central Louisiana coast from the Mississippi River Delta to Marsh Island near Atchafalaya Bay. It stretched from shallow, near shore water, 10-1 5 feet, to waters as deep as 60 feet. It seems that the persistent winds from the southwest and west pushed the nutrient-rich freshwater eastward and held it on the central and eastern Louisiana shelf. The weather pattern observed across the southern U.S. this spring and summer helped to shape this distribution. From 1993 to 1997, the dead zone covered 6,500 to 7,000 square miles of the Gulf from the Mississippi River to the upper Texas coast.

The earliest fossil sciaenid, Eocilophyodus, is from the upper Cretaceous of West Africa, and later fossils are from North America and Europe (Romer, 1966). The fossil record suggests the sciaenid radiation occurred during late Mesozoic to early Cenozoic and was strong in the New World. The Tethys and Trans-American Seas were open at that time allowing dispersal of sciaenids into their present worldwide distribution, which is temperate to tropical. Pleistocene climatic changes affected distribution of temperate water shore fishes in the Florida area (2083). During cold glacial periods they were able to extend their ranges around the southern tip of Florida to inhabit both the Gulf and western Atlantic waters. Warm waters of interglacial periods then forced them northward from southern Florida along both sides of the peninsula thereby isolating the ends of their distributions (1744).  Following the last glacial maximum about 18,000 years ago, the sea level has risen to its present stand, and repopulation of shelf, bays, and estuaries has taken place in the northern Gulf of Mexico. New tropical immigrants brought in by the Gulf Loop Current, and possible other means (1908, 1905) have been added to the biota of the
Northern Gulf (1904). Considering the variability of the environments, and the periodic addition of new faunal elements from the south, it is reasonable to conclude that the processes of genetic adjustment are still underway (1904).

This conclusion is supported by the fact that several key species of this ecological system appear to exhibit R-type life history strategies.  They are opportunistic pioneering species with short life history and high reproductive rate. They are adapted for rapid exploitation of new ecological opportunities and for persistence in the area despite local habitat loss, great variability in environmental factors, and the occasional occurrence of natural catastrophic events. These key species include brown and white shrimp, blue crab, gulf menhaden, sand seatrout, spot, Atlantic croaker, and striped mullet, all estuary-dependent, as well as the longspine porgy, a non-estuary dependent species, and several non-estuary dependent flatfish (1904). These species have persisted and flourished in the area and have contributed to the stability of the shelf ecological system.

Biochemical systematics study of soluble proteins suggested that C. nebulosus is the most diverged seatrout of the four Cynoscion species of the north Atlantic (1290). Karyologic and eight enzyme systems analyzed with one buffer in fish from the northern Gulf showed: diploid chromosome number 2n = 48 = 1 metacentric pair + 46 acrocentric pairs. Fundamental Number (FN) = 50. Five of the 16 loci assayed were distinct in a comparison to C. arenarius, but genetic distance indicated that they are closer to each other than the average genetic distance for other congeneric species (1801). Genetic identification of spring-spawned eggs in the lower Chesapeake bay was accomplished by Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (RFLP) of mitochondria1 DNA (mtDNA).This study suggested that OED (outside egg diameter) analysis are subject to error (Daniel &Graves, 1994).

A rapid method for preparing and reading thin sections of large otoliths, >3 mm in diameter, was described. This method uses a thin-sectioning machine equipped with both a cut-off saw and a calibrated precision grinder with aluminum guide arms for feeding otoliths mounted to petrographic glass slides. This machine allows an experienced technician to quickly prepare and read otoliths without sacrificing quality and precision (1654).

Moshin (1765) described the otoliths of the weakfishes, genus Cynoscion, of the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the U.S. The otoliths of the spotted seatrout are described in detail and specific differences with other species are observed. Based on otolith morphology two phyletic lines were postulated; the first one includes C. nebulosus and C. arenarius, and the second one comprises C. nothus and C regalis (1765).

The spotted seatrout is placed in the tribe Cynoscionini. This suprageneric group is characterized by having a simple swim bladder with a pair of anterior, horn-shaped diverticula and no barbells on chin (2086).

Kostecki (1697) mentioned the following special considerations: 1. Spotted seatrout is tolerant of relatively wide variations in environmental conditions; this tolerance may permit the species to occupy a niche that is intolerable to most marine predators and competitors (701).  However, to what degree the absence or presence of competitors affects the carrying capacity of a particular habitat is unknown. 2. Because few spotted seatrout move from one estuary to another, losses of larval and juvenile fish can result in the loss of that year class to the fishery.  Population increases by outside recruitment is not a factor (1281).

The percent of survival of tagged spotted seatrout was 75% in Florida Bay (1672). This study used internal anchored spaghetti tags. A comparison between tagged and untagged fish showed no significant difference. Also, transport the fish up to 16 km from the point of capture did not significantly decrease survival in tagged or untagged fish (1672). Short term survivability of tagged spotted seatrout in marine waters of the Everglades National Park was studied. Survival was related to the method of fish capture. Mortality was 45% and 5% for fish caught in nets and angling respectively (1756).

Abundance of juvenile spotted seatrout was reported for Tampa Bay, Charlotte Harbor, Indian River Lagoon, and Choctawhatchee Bay. An index of relative abundance of juveniles was developed and in the future may permit predictions of anticipated stock size (1674).

Abnormalities. A 302 mm SL pugheaded spotted seatrout was captured in Lake Chavin, Louisiana on April 3, 1968. It was suggested that growth rate was apparently slowed due to reduced feeding efficiency caused by pugheadedness (1774).

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content: Title: Spotted Seatrout (Cynoscion nebulosus)

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
